questions.q: Which async Apex option does this lesson recommend for processing a large number of records through a callout-driven process in controlled-size chunks?
options: Future methods
Batch Apex
A synchronous trigger
A Named Credential
questions.explain: Batch Apex is specifically suited to processing large record volumes through a callout-driven process in manageable chunks, which fits Doverfield's planned bulk-requote initiative.

questions.q: What capability does Queueable Apex offer that a Future method does not?
options: Queueable Apex can chain one job into another and accept more complex input than a Future method's primitive-only parameters
Queueable Apex is the only async pattern that can make any callout at all
Queueable Apex removes the 100-callout-per-transaction limit entirely
Future methods can only be used for DML, never callouts
questions.explain: The distinguishing feature of Queueable over Future methods is chaining support and more flexible input types, useful when a callout's result needs to trigger a further dependent async step.

questions.q: What does a circuit breaker pattern do once failures against an external dependency cross a threshold?
options: It permanently disables the integration with no way to resume
It 'opens' and short-circuits further calls to that dependency immediately with a known fallback response, instead of spending a full timeout window on calls likely to fail
It automatically increases the callout timeout to 120 seconds
It deletes the Named Credential associated with that dependency
questions.explain: An open circuit fails fast with a fallback instead of waiting out a timeout on calls that are very likely to fail, and after a cooldown it allows limited test calls through to check whether the dependency has recovered.

questions.q: Why does this lesson say a shorter timeout value alone doesn't make a design resilient?
options: Because timeouts cannot be configured in Apex at all
Because a shorter timeout just fails faster -- the actual resilience question is what fallback behavior happens after the timeout or failure, which a timeout value alone doesn't define
Because shortening a timeout always increases the 100-callout limit
Because Salesforce ignores timeout settings below 120 seconds
questions.explain: A fast failure with no defined fallback is still a failure with no path forward -- resilience comes from pairing the timeout with an explicit fallback behavior, not from the timeout value itself.

questions.q: Why would plain Future methods be a poor fit for Doverfield's 5,000-quote bulk-requote initiative?
options: Future methods cannot make callouts under any circumstances
Future methods are designed for simple, independent, one-off callouts, not for processing a large volume of records in controlled, manageable chunks the way Batch Apex is built to do
Future methods are deprecated and no longer supported by Salesforce
Future methods automatically fail after exactly 100 invocations
questions.explain: Future methods fit a simple independent callout, not large-volume chunked processing -- Batch Apex's chunking design is the better fit for thousands of records processed overnight.
